evaluations.name: Correctness parity
evaluations.prompt: Score the correctness of behavior this repository currently implements and claims to support against stable public PyTorch, from 0 to 100. Missing APIs belong exclusively to the separate PyTorch feature coverage evaluation and must not lower this correctness score. Inspect executable Rust, Python, and differential tests and their implementation evidence. Evaluate outputs, shapes, strides, dtypes, devices, errors, aliasing and view semantics, numerical edge cases, autograd behavior, empty tensors, and interactions among supported features. A score of 100 means the supported surface is indistinguishable from PyTorch and comprehensively edge-tested; any regression in previously supported behavior must lower the score. Use the latest applicable point in docs/burner-evaluation-history.json as numeric calibration for the code revision it measured: preserve that credit when relevant code and evidence are unchanged, and move it only for concrete changes since that revision.

evaluations.name: PyTorch feature coverage
evaluations.prompt: Score weighted PyTorch feature coverage from 0 to 100 using the fixed area weights and rules in FEATURES.md. Count only stable public Python concepts backed by executable side-by-side semantic tests; Rust-only capabilities, stubs, documentation-only claims, and missing edge-case behavior do not count. Include tensor storage and views, dtypes/devices/dispatch, creation and math, linear algebra, autograd, neural-network APIs, optimizers and data utilities, serialization, compilation and distributed execution, and ecosystem ergonomics. Missing capabilities remain zero in their denominator. Use the latest applicable point in docs/burner-evaluation-history.json as numeric calibration for the code revision it measured: preserve that credit when relevant code and evidence are unchanged, and move it only for concrete changes since that revision.

evaluations.name: Performance parity
evaluations.prompt: Score performance parity of behavior this repository currently implements and claims to support against equivalent PyTorch operations, from 0 to 100. Missing APIs belong exclusively to the separate PyTorch feature coverage evaluation and must not lower this performance score; incorrect supported behavior still receives zero performance credit. Apply BENCHMARKING.md: compare equivalent work, release/native execution, symmetric warmup and sampling, representative shapes/layouts/thread counts, geometric aggregation, and protection against dead-code elimination or deferred work. Credit concrete implementation and benchmark evidence rather than isolated favorable microkernels. A score of 100 means the supported workload is broadly at parity with or faster than PyTorch without semantic shortcuts. Use the latest applicable point in docs/burner-evaluation-history.json as numeric calibration for the code revision it measured: preserve that credit when relevant code and evidence are unchanged, and move it only for concrete changes since that revision.

evaluations.name: Python API compatibility
evaluations.prompt: Score drop-in compatibility of the torch_rs Python API with stable public PyTorch from 0 to 100. Inspect the exported namespace, function and method signatures, argument forms and defaults, return types, Tensor properties, dtype/device metadata, exception behavior, scalar and sequence handling, views and aliasing, autograd-facing behavior, modules, and ordinary import/package ergonomics. Award credit only for implemented behavior supported by executable compatibility tests, and keep the deliberately unsupported PyTorch surface in the denominator. Use the latest applicable point in docs/burner-evaluation-history.json as numeric calibration for the code revision it measured: preserve that credit when relevant code and evidence are unchanged, and move it only for concrete changes since that revision.

evaluations.name: Benchmark integrity
evaluations.prompt: Score the integrity and decision quality of the repository's correctness and performance evidence from 0 to 100. Apply README.md and BENCHMARKING.md: evaluators must be independent from implementation branches, equivalent work must be compared, incorrect and unsupported cells must score zero, seeds and held-out shapes must resist specialization, outputs must be materialized, provenance and environment must be reported, and quick screens must remain strict subsets of final gates. Credit enforced tests and workflows over prose, and penalize editable, asymmetric, gameable, noisy, or irreproducible measurements. Use the latest applicable point in docs/burner-evaluation-history.json as numeric calibration for the code revision it measured: preserve that credit when relevant code and evidence are unchanged, and move it only for concrete changes since that revision.

evaluations.name: Sustainable architecture
evaluations.prompt: Score how sustainably the native Rust engine can grow toward broad PyTorch semantics from 0 to 100. Inspect storage/layout/view abstractions, dtype and device dispatch boundaries, operation reuse, autograd graph design, Python bindings, safety, error consistency, modularity, tests, and dependency discipline. Reward clear extensible mechanisms that preserve existing fast paths and semantics. Penalize monolithic dispatch, duplicated per-operation logic, benchmark-specific branches, forwarding production operations to Python or PyTorch, fragile special cases, and architecture that makes the next feature disproportionately risky. Use the latest applicable point in docs/burner-evaluation-history.json as numeric calibration for the code revision it measured: preserve that credit when relevant code and evidence are unchanged, and move it only for concrete changes since that revision.

evaluations.name: Default torch.compile program coverage
evaluations.prompt: Run the versioned public-default-compile-v2 executable gate documented in docs/torch-compile-default-evaluator.md. Compare framework.compile(program) with no backend, fullgraph, dynamic, mode, or options override, against the locked PyTorch 2.13 default Inductor backend. The fixed representative corpus has 28 programs in 14 weighted categories, two input/shape variants, a same-shape changed-value check, CPU and real CUDA execution, and required output/metadata/alias/gradient checks. All 112 program/variant/device cells remain in the denominator. A reference or infrastructure failure invalidates the measurement; candidate unsupported, incorrect, or original-body eager execution receives zero. Never substitute backend='eager', a custom reference backend, benchmark tensor wrappers, a private fixed kernel, historical timings, or an LLM estimate for this command. Report only the measured weighted corpus percentage; it is not a percentage of all possible Python programs. This is a metric correction: legacy v2 scores are non-comparable and must not calibrate this version or count as candidate implementation gains/regressions.

evaluations.name: Default torch.compile CUDA performance
evaluations.prompt: Run the versioned public-default-compile-v2 CUDA performance gate in docs/torch-compile-default-evaluator.md on an available real NVIDIA GPU. Compare ordinary public torch_rs.compile(program) and default PyTorch 2.13 torch.compile(program), with no backend/mode/options overrides, across the same 28 programs and two variants (56 fixed CUDA cells). Require complete output/metadata/alias/gradient correctness, same-shape changed-input verification, ordinary native CUDA tensors, no installed-PyTorch forwarding, and no eager replay of the original Python body. Use identical runtime synchronization, five warmups, 17 samples, one host thread, separate fresh processes and caches, both implementation orders, and separate cold versus steady timings. Cap each successful cell's reference/candidate median-latency ratio at one; failed or unsupported cells receive zero. Aggregate capped ratios geometrically within the 14 fixed-weight categories and report common-success geometric mean separately (null when no cells pass). Any reference/infrastructure failure invalidates the run; do not remove workloads. The legacy four-shape prepared-executor microbenchmark is a non-scoring specialized diagnostic, not evidence for this default comparison. Legacy v1 100 scores are non-comparable: require a fresh baseline without carrying score floors or attributing this metric correction to implementation changes.

evaluations.name: Repository polish
evaluations.prompt: Score repository polish from 0 to 100 from the perspective of a new contributor or adopter. Inspect top-level organization, README.md, focused documentation, navigation, installation and first-success instructions, architecture explanation, supported-versus-unsupported scope, testing and benchmarking guidance, contribution workflow, examples, naming consistency, generated artifacts, and general repository hygiene. Reward concise progressive disclosure, a short useful README that routes readers to focused documents, accurate runnable examples, clear ownership boundaries, discoverable tooling, and maintained documentation that matches executable behavior. Penalize README sprawl that reads like an exhaustive changelog or API dump, repetitive or generated-looking prose, stale or contradictory claims, weak information hierarchy, undocumented setup assumptions, scattered guidance, noisy tracked artifacts, and cosmetic reshuffling without improved comprehension. Do not reward documentation volume; preserve necessary compatibility contracts while moving detail to the right durable location. Ground the score in concrete repository evidence and usability checks. A score of 100 means the repository feels deliberate, concise, navigable, and release-quality to an external engineer. Use the latest applicable point in docs/burner-evaluation-history.json as numeric calibration for the code revision it measured: preserve that credit when relevant files and evidence are unchanged, and move it only for concrete changes since that revision.

evaluations.name: Hardware heterogeneity
evaluations.prompt: Score accelerator hardware heterogeneity from 0 to 100 using the fixed v1 backend and capability matrix in docs/hardware-heterogeneity-evaluator.md and docs/hardware-heterogeneity-matrix-v1.json. For each NVIDIA CUDA, AMD ROCm, Apple MPS, Intel XPU, Google TPU/XLA, Intel Gaudi HPU, and Meta MTIA family, score the weighted fraction of reference-eligible stable PyTorch 2.13 behavior that torch_rs executes correctly on that accelerator across device tensors/transfers, dtypes/layout/views, math/reductions/linear algebra, autograd/training, neural networks/optimizers, RNG/serialization, compilation, and multi-device/distributed behavior. Average the seven backend scores equally and report both that feature-depth score and the unweighted backend-breadth percentage. A cell earns credit only from executable differential tests on real corresponding hardware, or reproducible commit-bound hardware CI/release evidence when that hardware is unavailable locally. Device parsing, availability flags, metadata shims, cross-compilation, emulation, CPU fallback, installed-PyTorch forwarding, documentation claims, and private one-workload benchmark paths do not establish general backend support; award only the exact cases they prove. Missing, skipped, unsupported, stale, or unverifiable cases stay in the denominator as zero. This host has real NVIDIA H100 GPUs, so inspect or run CUDA-relevant tests with CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 rather than assuming CUDA is unavailable. A score of 100 means full tested parity across every reference-eligible matrix cell on all seven accelerator families. Use the latest applicable point in docs/burner-evaluation-history.json as numeric calibration for the code revision it measured: preserve that credit when relevant code and evidence are unchanged, and move it only for concrete changes since that revision.
